courses.title: Obstetrics
courses.description: Antenatal care, normal and abnormal labour, obstetric haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, medical disorders in pregnancy and the puerperium.

topics.title: Antenatal Care and Normal Pregnancy
topics.summary: Physiological changes, booking, routine investigations, and prevention strategies.

material.heading: Physiology and booking
material.body: Pregnancy increases plasma volume (~40–50%) more than red cell mass, causing physiological haemodilution (Hb < 11 g/dL is anaemia in pregnancy); cardiac output rises by ~40%; hypercoagulability increases thromboembolism risk; insulin resistance develops in later pregnancy; GFR rises (lower creatinine). Gestational age: Naegele's rule (EDD = LMP + 9 months + 7 days), confirmed by early ultrasound. Booking visit (ideally before 12 weeks): history (previous pregnancies, medical conditions), examination, BP, weight/BMI, urinalysis, and investigations — FBC, blood group and antibodies, haemoglobin genotype, HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis (VDRL/RPR), urine culture, and blood glucose where indicated. WHO recommends at least 8 contacts. Routine interventions in Nigeria: iron and folic acid, IPTp with SP (from 13 weeks, monthly), insecticide-treated nets, tetanus–diphtheria vaccine, deworming after the first trimester, calcium supplementation where intake is low, and birth preparedness and complication readiness.
keyPoints: Plasma volume ↑ > red cells → Hb < 11 anaemia

material.heading: Fetal assessment and danger signs
material.body: Symphysis–fundal height (cm) approximates gestational weeks from about 24 weeks. Fetal well-being is assessed by fetal movements (reduced movements need prompt assessment), auscultation of the fetal heart (normal baseline 110–160 bpm), ultrasound (growth, liquor, placenta), cardiotocography and umbilical artery Doppler. Lie, presentation and engagement are assessed in late pregnancy (Leopold manoeuvres). Danger signs for which women should seek care immediately: vaginal bleeding, severe headache or blurred vision, convulsions, severe abdominal pain, fever, reduced fetal movements, leaking liquor, and swelling of face and hands. Prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV (PMTCT): maternal ART (TLD), infant prophylaxis and early infant diagnosis; hepatitis B birth-dose vaccine and immunoglobulin (and tenofovir for mothers with high viral load).
keyPoints: HBV: birth dose + tenofovir if high VL

topics.title: Labour and Delivery
topics.summary: Stages of labour, partograph, fetal monitoring, malpresentation and operative delivery.

material.heading: Normal labour
material.body: Labour is regular painful contractions causing progressive cervical dilatation and effacement. First stage: latent (to 5 cm by WHO 2018 guidance) and active (5 cm to full dilatation; progress about ≥ 1 cm/hour traditionally, though WHO's Labour Care Guide allows more individualised limits); second stage: full dilatation to delivery of the baby (prolonged if > 2 hours in primigravidae without epidural); third stage: delivery of the placenta — active management (AMTSL: oxytocin 10 IU IM after birth, controlled cord traction, uterine massage) prevents PPH. The partograph (and the newer WHO Labour Care Guide) records progress, fetal heart and maternal condition, with alert and action lines. Mechanism of labour (occipitoanterior): engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, external rotation and expulsion. Supportive care: companion of choice, mobility, oral fluids, and pain relief.

material.heading: Abnormal labour and operative delivery
material.body: Causes of prolonged or obstructed labour: the 3 Ps — powers (inefficient contractions — augment with oxytocin if no obstruction), passenger (malposition — occipitoposterior; malpresentation — breech, brow, face, shoulder/transverse lie; macrosomia) and passage (cephalopelvic disproportion, contracted pelvis in young adolescents). Obstructed labour causes uterine rupture, obstetric fistula (vesicovaginal — common in northern Nigeria), sepsis and fetal death; signs include moulding, caput, Bandl's ring and haematuria. Fetal distress: abnormal fetal heart rate (late decelerations, persistent bradycardia), meconium-stained liquor. Operative delivery: vacuum or forceps (full dilatation, head engaged, known position) and caesarean section (lower segment preferred; indications include obstructed labour, previous CS with contraindication to VBAC, placenta praevia, fetal distress, malpresentation). Shoulder dystocia is managed with McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure (HELPERR). Breech delivery by skilled attendants or caesarean section.

topics.title: Obstetric Haemorrhage
topics.summary: Early pregnancy bleeding, antepartum haemorrhage and postpartum haemorrhage.

material.heading: Early pregnancy and antepartum haemorrhage
material.body: Bleeding in early pregnancy: miscarriage (threatened — closed os; inevitable/incomplete — open os; complete; missed), ectopic pregnancy (amenorrhoea, abdominal pain, bleeding; ruptured ectopic causes shock — urgent laparotomy; unruptured may be treated with methotrexate or laparoscopy), molar pregnancy (very high hCG, 'snowstorm' ultrasound; evacuation and hCG follow-up), and unsafe abortion complications (sepsis, haemorrhage, uterine perforation — a major cause of maternal death in Nigeria; post-abortion care with MVA or misoprostol). Antepartum haemorrhage (bleeding after 28 weeks): placenta praevia (painless bright red bleeding, soft non-tender uterus, malpresentation; confirm with ultrasound; NEVER do digital vaginal examination; caesarean delivery) and placental abruption (painful bleeding, tense tender 'woody' uterus, fetal distress, shock disproportionate to visible blood loss, DIC; associated with hypertension). Vasa praevia and local causes are rarer.

material.heading: Postpartum haemorrhage
material.body: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH): blood loss ≥ 500 mL after vaginal birth (≥ 1,000 mL after caesarean) within 24 hours (primary) or after 24 hours to 12 weeks (secondary — retained products, infection). It is the leading cause of maternal death in Nigeria. Causes — the 4 Ts: Tone (uterine atony — the commonest; risk factors include prolonged labour, overdistension — twins, polyhydramnios, macrosomia — grand multiparity, and infection), Trauma (tears, uterine rupture, inversion), Tissue (retained placenta or fragments) and Thrombin (coagulopathy). Management (WHO E-MOTIVE bundle — early detection with calibrated drapes, then Massage, Oxytocics, Tranexamic acid within 3 hours, IV fluids, Examination and Escalation): call for help, uterine massage, oxytocin infusion, ergometrine (avoid in hypertension), misoprostol, carboprost, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, bimanual compression, examine for trauma, remove retained products, transfuse, and escalate to balloon tamponade (condom catheter), B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation or hysterectomy. Non-pneumatic anti-shock garments help during transfer.

topics.title: Hypertensive and Medical Disorders in Pregnancy
topics.summary: Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, gestational diabetes, anaemia, sickle cell disease and infections in pregnancy.

material.heading: Hypertensive disorders
material.body: Hypertensive disorders include chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension (new BP ≥ 140/90 after 20 weeks without proteinuria), pre-eclampsia (new hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or other organ dysfunction — renal, liver, neurological, haematological, or fetal growth restriction) and eclampsia (seizures). Severe features: BP ≥ 160/110, headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets), pulmonary oedema, oliguria. Management: antihypertensives (oral nifedipine, labetalol, methyldopa; IV hydralazine or labetalol for severe hypertension), magnesium sulfate for prevention and treatment of seizures (Pritchard IM or Zuspan IV regimens; monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output; antidote calcium gluconate), and delivery — the definitive treatment (timing by gestation and severity; steroids for fetal lung maturity < 34 weeks). Low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks prevents pre-eclampsia in high-risk women; calcium supplementation where dietary intake is low.

material.heading: Medical disorders
material.body: Gestational diabetes (GDM): screen with OGTT at 24–28 weeks in at-risk women; diet and exercise, then metformin or insulin; risks include macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycaemia and later type 2 diabetes. Anaemia (iron deficiency, malaria, hookworm, HIV) — iron supplements, IV iron or transfusion if severe. Sickle cell disease in pregnancy is high risk (crises, acute chest syndrome, pre-eclampsia, growth restriction, maternal death) — multidisciplinary care, folic acid, malaria prophylaxis, hydration, and prophylactic LMWH. Malaria in pregnancy causes anaemia, low birth weight and stillbirth — IPTp, ITNs and prompt ACT treatment. HIV: lifelong ART and viral suppression before delivery. Urinary tract infections (asymptomatic bacteriuria should be treated — risk of pyelonephritis and preterm labour). Heart disease (rheumatic mitral stenosis; peripartum cardiomyopathy). Thromboprophylaxis for high-risk women.

topics.title: Preterm Labour, Puerperium and Maternal Mortality
topics.summary: Preterm birth, PROM, puerperal sepsis, postnatal care and preventing maternal death.

material.heading: Preterm labour and PROM
material.body: Preterm birth (< 37 weeks) is the leading cause of neonatal death. Risk factors: previous preterm birth, infections (UTI, malaria, chorioamnionitis), multiple pregnancy, cervical insufficiency, antepartum haemorrhage, pre-eclampsia and young maternal age. Management of threatened preterm labour (24–34 weeks): antenatal corticosteroids (dexamethasone 6 mg IM 12-hourly × 4 doses or betamethasone 12 mg × 2 doses) to reduce respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and death; tocolysis (nifedipine) to allow steroids to act; magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection before 32 weeks; antibiotics for GBS where indicated; and delivery where neonatal care is available. Premature rupture of membranes (PROM): confirm by speculum (pooling of liquor); preterm PROM — erythromycin, steroids, monitor for chorioamnionitis (fever, tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor), avoid digital examinations; term PROM — induction of labour.

material.heading: Puerperium and maternal mortality
material.body: The puerperium is the 6 weeks after delivery. Postnatal care checks (within 24 hours, day 3, 1–2 weeks and 6 weeks): bleeding (lochia), uterine involution, BP, infection, breastfeeding, mental health (baby blues vs postnatal depression vs puerperal psychosis — emergency), family planning (postpartum IUD, implants) and newborn care. Puerperal sepsis (fever, offensive lochia, tender uterus — after prolonged labour, unhygienic delivery, retained products, CS) is a leading cause of maternal death: broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin, gentamicin, metronidazole), evacuate retained products, drain collections. Other complications: breast engorgement, mastitis and abscess, VTE, secondary PPH. Nigeria has one of the world's highest maternal mortality ratios; reducing it requires family planning, skilled birth attendance, emergency obstetric care, blood availability, addressing the three delays, and maternal death reviews (MPDSR).
